name: Afimoxifene (4-hydroxytamoxifen)
lead: Afimoxifene, also called 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT), is an active metabolite of tamoxifen and a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM). It has been developed as a topical gel, under the tentative brand name TamoGel, so that the drug can act on breast tissue through the skin [1].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities it comes up as a topical option for gynecomastia, the enlargement of glandular breast tissue in men, where a flatter, leaner chest is the appearance goal. The chain people describe is local estrogen-receptor blocking in the chest, then less glandular tissue, then a cleaner chest line. Published trials of the gel have been in women, for cyclical breast pain, breast density and breast cancer settings; no trial in men with gynecomastia has been identified [2][3].

Tamoxifen itself is a prodrug that the body converts into 4-hydroxytamoxifen and endoxifen, which bind the estrogen receptor with roughly 100-fold greater affinity than the parent drug [9]. Afimoxifene is that more active form, formulated for application to the skin.

paras: Afimoxifene acts on estrogen receptors alpha and beta, with estrogen-like or estrogen-blocking effects depending on the tissue. It also binds the G protein-coupled estrogen receptor with much lower affinity than estradiol, and antagonises the estrogen-related receptors ERR-beta and ERR-gamma [1]. Its sulfation by human sulfotransferases, notably SULT1A1 and SULT1C4, has been characterised in lab work alongside endoxifen, raloxifene and fulvestrant [4].

Oral tamoxifen requires activation by cytochrome P450 enzymes, chiefly CYP2D6, to form 4-hydroxytamoxifen and endoxifen. Genetic variants and interacting drugs that affect CYP2D6 change the blood levels of these metabolites and have been linked to differences in treatment outcomes [9]. Steady-state levels of tamoxifen and its metabolites in breast cancer patients were described in a 1986 pharmacokinetic study [15].

The rationale for applying the active metabolite directly to the skin of the breast is to reach local tissue while limiting the whole-body exposure and side effects associated with oral tamoxifen. Researchers have evaluated this local transdermal approach for breast cancer prevention and DCIS therapy in preclinical and clinical work [10].

The gel has been developed for breast hyperplasia and has completed a Phase II trial for cyclical mastalgia; Wikipedia notes more studies are needed before approval for that use [1]. Registered trials have also examined topical afimoxifene for mammographic breast density, ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), atypical hyperplasia, and in breast cancer survivors after radiation [5][6][7][11][13].
No regulator has approved afimoxifene for any use, and it is not marketed as a medicine. Its appearance-related use in male communities is off-label and unstudied.

A Phase II randomised trial in premenopausal women compared two doses of 4-OHT gel with placebo gel for moderate to severe cyclical mastalgia; its stated aim was to assess safety and efficacy with a lower risk of the side effects associated with oral tamoxifen [2]. The registration lists 146 participants and a 2003 start [3].

Further registered studies include a Phase III trial on mammographic density (terminated) [6], a Phase II trial in women with dense breasts (194 participants) [5], Phase II trials in DCIS [7][12], an earlier study of gel effects on breast density, salivary sex steroids and quality of life in premenopausal women [14], and a Phase II study in breast cancer survivors after radiation of one breast [11]. No studies in men with gynecomastia, and none on appearance outcomes, were found.

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On bodybuilding forums such as T Nation, tamoxifen and related SERMs are discussed mainly in the context of gynecomastia and post-cycle recovery. Posters have debated tamoxifen's tissue-dependent effects, including its estrogen-agonist action in the uterus attributed to the 4-hydroxytamoxifen metabolite [16], and whether tamoxifen is counterproductive in post-cycle use [17]. These discussions concern oral tamoxifen; afimoxifene gel is mentioned as a topical alternative.
Afimoxifene is investigational and not approved as a medicine; supplies outside clinical trials are not a regulated product.

timeline.event: Phase II trial of afimoxifene gel in cyclical mastalgia begins [8].
Phase II study of 4-hydroxytamoxifen or tamoxifen in newly diagnosed DCIS begins [12].
Phase II DCIS trial and Phase III breast-density trial of the gel begin [6][7].
Phase II trial in breast cancer survivors after radiation begins [11].

card.summary: The active form of tamoxifen, studied as a breast gel in women; use for male gynecomastia has no published trials.

quick.overview:
Afimoxifene is the active metabolite of tamoxifen, formulated as a gel for application to the breast. It remains investigational.
Trials have been in women for breast pain, density and cancer settings. Its use for male gynecomastia, which is how it comes up in these communities, has not been tested in published trials found.
quick.mechanism: A SERM that blocks or mimics estrogen at estrogen receptors depending on the tissue; applied topically, the aim is local breast effects.
quick.risks: Side-effect details for the gel were not reviewed in depth; the mastalgia trial was designed around avoiding the systemic effects of oral tamoxifen.
